theory.title: IXP: Where the Internet Physically Meets
theory.recap: BGP peers exchange routes between Autonomous Systems. But peering requires a physical connection between the two networks' routers. When two ISPs want to exchange traffic, they need a place to connect - and that place is an Internet Exchange Point.
theory.plainObjective: Two ISPs (AS-A and AS-B) are connected at an IXP. The direct peering path through the IXP is faster and cheaper than the transit path through the transit provider. Route via the IXP.
theory.summary: IXPs are the physical meeting points of the internet. Amsterdam's AMS-IX exchanges over 10 Tbps. Frankfurt's DE-CIX is the world's largest. By peering at an IXP instead of paying a transit provider, ISPs cut costs and reduce latency - packets travel fewer hops.

bodyParagraphs.heading: What is an IXP?
bodyParagraphs.text: An Internet Exchange Point is a data center where many networks connect to a shared switch. Instead of each pair of ISPs running a private cable, everyone connects to the IXP and peers with any other member. One connection, many peers.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Peering vs transit
bodyParagraphs.text:
• Peering - two networks exchange traffic directly, typically for free
  • Transit - a smaller network pays a larger network to carry its traffic to the rest of the internet
IXPs facilitate peering. Transit is the alternative when no peering agreement exists.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Why IXPs reduce latency
bodyParagraphs.text: Without an IXP, traffic between two local ISPs might travel to a transit backbone and back, adding hundreds of milliseconds. Through an IXP, the same traffic stays local: two hops instead of ten.

bodyParagraphs.heading: BGP at the IXP
bodyParagraphs.text: At an IXP, members run BGP sessions via a shared route server. The route server collects and distributes prefixes so each member doesn't need a direct BGP session with every other member.

theory.mission:
Your packet travels from a client in AS-A's network to a server in AS-B's network (203.0.113.10).

Two paths exist: through the transit provider (expensive, more hops) or through the IXP (direct peering, fewer hops). The BGP table in AS-A prefers the IXP path for AS-B's prefixes. Route via the IXP.

termIntroductions.headline: IXP
termIntroductions.body: An Internet Exchange Point is a shared physical infrastructure where ISPs and networks connect and peer. Instead of each pair of networks paying for a private connection, everyone plugs into the IXP switch. DE-CIX in Frankfurt exchanges over 14 Tbps - more than most countries' total internet traffic.

termIntroductions.headline: Peering vs Transit
termIntroductions.body: AS-A's BGP table prefers the IXP path (203.0.113.0/24 via ixp-peer) over the transit provider for this prefix. The transit route is the default (0.0.0.0/0) - used for everything without a specific peering agreement. The /24 route is more specific, so the IXP path wins.

termIntroductions.headline: The IXP Switching Fabric
termIntroductions.body: The IXP runs a large Ethernet switch (or modern optical fabric). AS-A and AS-B both plug in and establish BGP sessions with each other (or via the IXP's route server). Packets flow directly between them at local latency - no transit provider involved.
